title: Module 12 · Practice: stats and coordinates
text:
Work these in your module-12-stats project in Posit Cloud, or just read them. Every exercise uses penguins or data that comes with R, so the patterns are the same for everyone. The solutions are visible: try first, then open them.
library(tidyverse)
penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Colors that color-blind viewers can tell apart (more in Module 13)
options(ggplot2.discrete.fill = function() scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.8))

title: Module 12 · Practice: stats and coordinates
text:
D1 · Count → share (question A)
Goal. Which island has the largest share of Adelie penguins? (Session 1, slides 10 and 17.)
Your turn. Make a group and an outcome, then plot the share of each group with the outcome, groups down the side.

d1_data <- penguins %>%
  mutate(
    group = ___,                       # the islands
    has_outcome = ___                  # TRUE when the penguin is Adelie
  )

ggplot(d1_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "___")

Investigate. What total does each bar divide by? Why can islands of different sizes now be compared?






TipSolution






d1_data <- penguins %>%
  mutate(
    group = island,
    has_outcome = species == "Adelie"
  )

ggplot(d1_data, aes(y = group, fill = has_outcome)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Share of the island", y = NULL, fill = "Adelie")








Each bar divides by its own island’s total (Biscoe 168, Dream 124, Torgersen 52), so every bar runs from 0 to 1 and the unit “penguins” cancels. Torgersen is 100% Adelie; Dream about 45%; Biscoe about 26%.




D1+ · Read and discuss: counties or people? (no code to write)
The same numbers can be counted per county or per person. midwest (built into ggplot2) has one row per county in five Midwest states.
ggplot(midwest, aes(x = percbelowpoverty)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  labs(x = "% below poverty", y = "Counties")
ggplot(midwest, aes(x = percbelowpoverty, weight = poptotal)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2) +
  labs(x = "% below poverty", y = "People")










Talk. The left plot counts counties; the right counts people. Why do they look different? Which one answers “how many people live in poor counties?” (This is choosing the unit, the same idea as choosing the total. Source: ggplot2 book §5.2.)

title: Module 12 · Practice: stats and coordinates
section: D2 · A summary with its spread
text:
D2 · A summary with its spread
Goal. Show each species’ rate of heavy penguins (over 4000 g) with its standard error and its n. (Session 1, slides 13–16.)
Your turn. Finish the summary, then draw the rates with ±se.

d2_rates <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(body_mass_g) %>%
  mutate(has_outcome = body_mass_g > 4000) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rate = mean(has_outcome),
    se = ___                           # the se of a rate
  )

ggplot(d2_rates, aes(x = rate, y = species,
                     xmin = rate - se, xmax = rate + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3)

Investigate. Whose range is widest? Look at its n and its rate.






TipSolution






d2_rates <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(body_mass_g) %>%
  mutate(has_outcome = body_mass_g > 4000) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rate = mean(has_outcome),
    se = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n)
  )
d2_rates

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  species       n  rate      se
  <chr>     <int> <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Adelie      151 0.232 0.0343 
2 Chinstrap    68 0.221 0.0503 
3 Gentoo      123 0.992 0.00810

ggplot(d2_rates, aes(x = rate, y = species,
                     xmin = rate - se, xmax = rate + se)) +
  geom_pointrange() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste("n =", n)), nudge_y = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Share heavier than 4000 g", y = NULL)








The se of a rate is sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n): it grows when n is small and when the rate is near 0.5. Chinstrap has the smallest n, so its range is wide; Gentoo’s rate is close to 1, so its range is narrow even with a similar n to Adelie.




D2b · A mean with its two spreads (Guided Project B2)

d2b <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(flipper_length_mm) %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(flipper_length_mm),
    sd = sd(flipper_length_mm),
    se = sd / sqrt(n)
  )
d2b

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  species       n  mean    sd    se
  <chr>     <int> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 Adelie      151  190.  6.54 0.532
2 Chinstrap    68  196.  7.13 0.865
3 Gentoo      123  217.  6.48 0.585


Investigate. Chinstrap’s mean is about 5.9 mm above Adelie’s. Big compared to the se? Compared to the sd? (Session 2, slide 7.)






TipSolution





Compared to the se (under 1 mm), 5.9 mm is large: we are confident the means differ. Compared to the sd (about 6.5–7 mm), it is less than one sd: many individual Adelie and Chinstrap penguins have similar flippers. Say which comparison you mean.





D2+ · Optional: see the noise (resampling)
Redraw the penguins with replacement 200 times and compute each species’ rate again. The width of each cloud is the uncertainty the se describes. (map() and slice_sample() are new; read and run, no need to write them.)

resamples <- map(1:200, \(i) {
  penguins %>%
    drop_na(body_mass_g) %>%
    slice_sample(prop = 1, replace = TRUE) %>%
    group_by(species) %>%
    summarize(rate = mean(body_mass_g > 4000))
}) %>%
  bind_rows(.id = "draw")

ggplot(resamples, aes(x = rate, y = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  labs(x = "Rate in each of 200 redraws", y = NULL)








Talk. Which species’ cloud is widest? Does that match D2’s ranges?

title: Module 12 · Practice: stats and coordinates
text:
D3 · Zoom or filter?
Goal. See what a zoomed axis does to bars, and compute its Lie Factor. (Session 2, slides 4–7.)
Your turn. Zoom the counts so the view starts at 40, then filter with the same limits.

d3_counts <- ggplot(penguins, aes(y = island)) +
  geom_bar()

d3_counts + ___(xlim = c(40, 175), expand = FALSE)   # zoom
d3_counts + ___(limits = c(40, 175))                 # filter

Investigate. Compute the Lie Factor of the zoomed plot for Biscoe (168) vs Torgersen (52).






TipSolution





d3_counts <- ggplot(penguins, aes(y = island)) +
  geom_bar()

d3_counts + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(40, 175), expand = FALSE)
d3_counts + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(40, 175))











drawn_ratio <- (168 - 40) / (52 - 40)
data_ratio <- 168 / 52
drawn_ratio / data_ratio

[1] 3.301587


The zoom keeps all the data but cuts the bars at 40: Biscoe looks about 10.7 times longer than Torgersen, while the counts differ 3.2 times, a Lie Factor of about 3.3. The filter removes the bars, because every bar starts at 0, outside the limits. Bars start at 0; to look closer, use points and say so.




D3+ · Compared to what? A narrow time window
economics (built into ggplot2) has monthly US data from 1967 to 2015.
economics %>%
  filter(date >= as.Date("2000-01-01"), date < as.Date("2008-01-01")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = unemploy / pop)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Unemployed per person, 2000–2007")
ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy / pop)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Unemployed per person, 1967–2015")










Talk. What story does the left plot tell on its own? What does the full series add? Why divide by pop? (Tufte’s “compared to what?” and standardized units, 2001, p. 77.)






TipSolution





The 2000–2007 window shows a rise and a fall that look dramatic; the full series shows they are small next to the peaks of the early 1980s and 2009. Dividing by the population makes years comparable: the number unemployed grows partly because the population grows.

title: Module 12 · Practice: stats and coordinates
text:
D4 · Change the frame
Goal. Ask question B (of all Adelie, what share lives on each island?) and compare the frames. (Session 1, slide 17; Session 2, slides 9–11.)
Your turn. Keep the Adelie, count per island, and turn the counts into shares of all Adelie. Draw them sideways.

d4_shares <- penguins %>%
  filter(species == "Adelie") %>%
  count(island) %>%
  mutate(share = ___)

ggplot(d4_shares, aes(x = share, y = island)) +
  geom_col()

Investigate. D1 said Torgersen is the “most Adelie” island. Does D4 agree?






TipSolution






d4_shares <- penguins %>%
  filter(species == "Adelie") %>%
  count(island) %>%
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))
d4_shares

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  island        n share
  <chr>     <int> <dbl>
1 Biscoe       44 0.289
2 Dream        56 0.368
3 Torgersen    52 0.342

ggplot(d4_shares, aes(x = share, y = island)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = "Share of all Adelie", y = NULL)








No: of all 152 Adelie, Dream holds the largest share (about 37%), Torgersen 34%, Biscoe 29%. Question A (÷ island total) and question B (÷ Adelie total) answer different questions; say which one you mean.




D4+ · Bar or pie?
p_share <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = "all", fill = species)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of all penguins")
p_share
p_share + coord_polar(theta = "y")










Talk. Adelie (44%) or Gentoo (36%): which is easier to compare on the bar, and on the pie? Why? (Tufte, 2001, p. 77: don’t show more dimensions than the data have.)






TipSolution





On the bar, both are lengths on one scale from 0 to 1, easy to compare. On the pie, you compare angles and areas, which people judge less accurately, especially when slices are close. The data have one dimension (a share per species); the pie spreads it over angle and area: more work for the reader, and no new information. Prefer the bar.




Data: Horst, A. M., Hill, A. P., & Gorman, K. B. (2020). palmerpenguins: Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica) penguin data (R package). midwest and economics come with ggplot2 (Wickham, Navarro & Pedersen, ggplot2, 3rd ed.).

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
NoteHow to use this page




Purpose: practice the three ideas from class in more depth. Each exercise is a pattern for one task in Guided Project 11: solve it here on penguins, then repeat the same moves on your own data.
Task: run the code in Posit Cloud: open practice/practice_d1-d4.R in the module-11-aes project (or download practice_d1-d4.R) and work section by section. About 15 minutes per exercise.
Success: you can answer each question before you open its answer, and your Modify and Make code draws the plot described.
Predictions are not graded anywhere. Answers are here so you can check yourself: try first, then open them.
What the measurement columns mean:
Every exercise starts the same way:
library(tidyverse)
penguins <- read_csv("data/penguins.csv")

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Predict
Bill length and bill depth: when one goes up, does the other go up or down? Will the answer change once each species gets its own color? Write your prediction before running anything.






TipShow answer





Look at the two plots below. Without color, the whole cloud tends to go down: longer bills look shallower. With color, within each species the points go up. The overall trend mixes three groups that sit in different places. Mapping the group to color reveals it.

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Run

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).








ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm,
                     color = species, shape = species)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Investigate

What does one point stand for? What does the warning in the console say, and why?
Why map species to both color and shape?
You will set alpha = 0.4 below. Why is alpha set (outside aes()) and not mapped?







TipShow answers






One penguin. Rows with a missing bill length or depth have no position, so geom_point() removes them and says so in the warning.
Two cues for the same column: the plot still reads in grayscale and for readers who do not see color differences (color is never the only cue).
Transparency here is not information about each penguin; it is one design choice for all points so overlaps show. One value for every mark is a setting.

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Modify
Map shape to island and set the transparency of every point to 0.4. Predict first: how many legends will there be?

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm,
                     color = species, shape = ___)) +
  geom_point(alpha = ___)







TipShow solution






ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm,
                     color = species, shape = island)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4)

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









Two legends: one for color (species) and one for shape (island). Alpha has no legend because it is set, not mapped.

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Make (choose one)

Option A (Body size): flipper_length_mm on x, body_mass_g on y, color mapped to sex.
Option B (Islands): body_mass_g on x, bill_depth_mm on y, color mapped to island, alpha set to 0.5.







TipShow solutions






ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g,
                     color = sex)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).








ggplot(penguins, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = bill_depth_mm,
                     color = island)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5)

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









Option A shows a third color for NA: penguins whose sex was not recorded. That is real missing data; D4 Option B shows one way to drop those rows.









ImportantPattern for Guided Project tasks A1 and B1



Choose two numeric columns of your dataset for x and y. Map one categorical column (in Fairness Data: the outcome or a sensitive attribute) to color. Your datasets have thousands of rows, so set alpha. Write first: *each row of my data is one ___*.

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Predict
penguins %>% count(island) makes a table. How many rows will it have, and how many columns will the plot below have?






TipShow answer





Three rows (Biscoe, Dream, Torgersen), so three columns: one mark per row.

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Run

island_counts <- penguins %>% count(island)
island_counts

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  island        n
  <chr>     <int>
1 Biscoe      168
2 Dream       124
3 Torgersen    52

ggplot(island_counts, aes(x = island, y = n)) +
  geom_col()

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Investigate

True or false: geom_col() counts the rows for you.
Run penguins %>% count(sex). Why are there three rows? What will the plot show for the third one?
geom_col() draws any number you computed, not only counts. Which function from Module 5 makes a table of means per group?







TipShow answers






False. count() did the counting; geom_col() draws the heights you give it. (geom_bar() counts for you because it computes a statistic: Module 12.)
The third row is NA: penguins whose sex was not recorded. The plot shows a column labeled NA. Missing values are data too.
group_by() + summarise().

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Modify
Draw the number of penguins measured in each year.

year_counts <- penguins %>% count(___)
ggplot(year_counts, aes(x = year, y = ___)) +
  geom_col()







TipShow solution






year_counts <- penguins %>% count(year)
ggplot(year_counts, aes(x = year, y = n)) +
  geom_col()

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Make (choose one)

Option A (Sexes): count penguins by sex and draw the counts.
Option B (Means, not counts): mean body_mass_g per species with group_by() + summarise(), drawn with geom_col().







TipShow solutions






sex_counts <- penguins %>% count(sex)
ggplot(sex_counts, aes(x = sex, y = n)) +
  geom_col()







species_mass <- penguins %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
ggplot(species_mass, aes(x = species, y = mean_mass)) +
  geom_col()

















ImportantPattern for Guided Project tasks A2 and B2



Pick one categorical column (an outcome, a sensitive attribute, a team, a position…). count() it, then draw the counts with geom_col(). Before plotting, print the small table: how many rows, so how many columns?

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Predict
penguin_means below has one row per species and year. Will the first plot show one line or three?






TipShow answer





One line that zigzags: nothing tells ggplot2 the rows belong to three species, so it joins all points in order of x and jumps up and down at each year.

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Run

penguin_means <- penguins %>%
  group_by(species, year) %>%
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")
penguin_means

# A tibble: 9 × 3
  species    year mean_mass
  <chr>     <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Adelie     2007     3696.
2 Adelie     2008     3742 
3 Adelie     2009     3665.
4 Chinstrap  2007     3694.
5 Chinstrap  2008     3800 
6 Chinstrap  2009     3725 
7 Gentoo     2007     5071.
8 Gentoo     2008     5020.
9 Gentoo     2009     5141.

ggplot(penguin_means, aes(x = year, y = mean_mass)) +
  geom_line()

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Investigate

How many rows does penguin_means have? Why that number?
Run both plots below. Which geom follows the order of the rows, and which sorts by x first?


walk <- tibble(step = c(1, 3, 2), place = c(10, 30, 15))
ggplot(walk, aes(x = step, y = place)) + geom_line()







ggplot(walk, aes(x = step, y = place)) + geom_path()









The x axis shows values like 2007.5. Is that a problem with the data or with the axis?







TipShow answers






Nine: 3 species × 3 years, one row per combination.
geom_path() follows the row order (1, 3, 2); geom_line() sorts by x (1, 2, 3). Minard’s map is a path: the army’s route, in order.
The axis: ggplot2 chose breaks for a continuous number. Changing breaks is part of scales (Module 13).

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Modify
Give each species its own line.

ggplot(penguin_means, aes(x = year, y = mean_mass, color = ___)) +
  geom_line()







TipShow solution






ggplot(penguin_means, aes(x = year, y = mean_mass, color = species)) +
  geom_line()








A discrete mapping (color) also makes groups, so there is one line per species. group = species would do the grouping without color.

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Make (choose one)

Option A (Flippers): mean flipper_length_mm per island and year, one line per island.
Option B (Counts over time): count(species, year), then one line per species showing how many penguins were measured each year.







TipShow solutions






flipper_means <- penguins %>%
  group_by(island, year) %>%
  summarise(mean_flipper = mean(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")
ggplot(flipper_means, aes(x = year, y = mean_flipper, color = island)) +
  geom_line()







species_year <- penguins %>% count(species, year)
ggplot(species_year, aes(x = year, y = n, color = species)) +
  geom_line()

















ImportantPattern for Guided Project task B3 (and A3 for Credit Card)



If your data has a time or order column (season, year, game number, round; Credit Card: month), summarise() one number per group and time point, then geom_line() with the group mapped to color. Check the number of rows first: groups × time points.

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Predict
species_centers has columns species, mean_flipper and mean_mass. The second layer below has no aes() of its own. Will it run?






TipShow answer





No. x and y are set in ggplot(), so every layer inherits them. The second layer looks for flipper_length_mm in species_centers, which does not have it.

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Run

species_centers <- penguins %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_flipper = mean(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
species_centers

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  species   mean_flipper mean_mass
  <chr>            <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Adelie            190.     3701.
2 Chinstrap         196.     3733.
3 Gentoo            217.     5076.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_point(data = species_centers, size = 5, shape = 4)

Error in `geom_point()`:
! Problem while computing aesthetics.
ℹ Error occurred in the 2nd layer.
Caused by error:
! object 'flipper_length_mm' not found

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Investigate

Read the error: which column is missing, and in which layer?
Fix it by giving the second layer its own aes(x = …, y = …). Which columns go there?
In the plot below, color = species is in ggplot(). Are the X marks colored? Why?


ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g,
                     color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_point(data = species_centers,
             aes(x = mean_flipper, y = mean_mass),
             size = 5, shape = 4)

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).















TipShow answers






flipper_length_mm, in the 2nd layer.
aes(x = mean_flipper, y = mean_mass): the columns of species_centers.
Yes. A mapping in ggplot() is global: every layer whose data has a species column uses it. Put color = species inside the first geom_point() to make it local to that layer.

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Modify
Add a third layer that writes each species’ name above its center.

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = species_centers,
             aes(x = mean_flipper, y = mean_mass),
             size = 5, shape = 4) +
  geom_text(data = ___,
            aes(x = mean_flipper, y = mean_mass, label = ___),
            vjust = -1.2)







TipShow solution






ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = species_centers,
             aes(x = mean_flipper, y = mean_mass),
             size = 5, shape = 4) +
  geom_text(data = species_centers,
            aes(x = mean_flipper, y = mean_mass, label = species),
            vjust = -1.2)

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).

title: Module 11 · Deeper practice D1–D4
text:
Make (choose one)

Option A (Islands): a scatter of bill_length_mm and bill_depth_mm colored by island, with each island’s mean bill length and depth as a large X and its name as a label.
Option B (Sexes): a scatter of flipper_length_mm and body_mass_g colored by sex, with a large X at the mean of each sex. Hint: drop the penguins with no recorded sex first, with filter(!is.na(sex)).







TipShow solutions






island_centers <- penguins %>%
  group_by(island) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_length = mean(bill_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_depth = mean(bill_depth_mm, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
ggplot(penguins, aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = island), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = island_centers,
             aes(x = mean_length, y = mean_depth),
             size = 5, shape = 4) +
  geom_text(data = island_centers,
            aes(x = mean_length, y = mean_depth, label = island),
            vjust = -1.2)

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).








penguins_sexed <- penguins %>% filter(!is.na(sex))
sex_centers <- penguins_sexed %>%
  group_by(sex) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_flipper = mean(flipper_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
ggplot(penguins_sexed, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = sex), alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(data = sex_centers,
             aes(x = mean_flipper, y = mean_mass),
             size = 5, shape = 4)

















ImportantPattern for Guided Project tasks A4 and B4



Layer 1: your scatter from A1/B1. Layer 2: a small table of group means (group_by() + summarise()) with its own aes(). Layer 3: geom_text() labels. In Fairness Data, check your dataset card first: a group with fewer than 30 rows gives an unreliable mean. Say so in your notes.



Data: Palmer Penguins (Horst, Hill & Gorman), CC0. Reference: Wickham, Navarro & Pedersen, ggplot2 (3e), chapters 2, 3 and 13.

title: Setup, Part 2: Connect Posit Cloud to GitHub
text:
In Part 1 you made your own repository on GitHub, turned on its website, and opened a working copy in Posit Cloud. Right now the copy only goes one way: from GitHub into Posit Cloud. In this tutorial you make it go both ways, so that the reports and slides you write in Posit Cloud reach GitHub and appear on your website. At the end, your home page shows your name at your own address.
You don’t need any experience with Git. Every step says what to click and what you should see. If something looks different, If something goes wrong lists the usual causes.











GitHub repository
Posit Cloud project




What it is
The shared copy. Public. Keeps the full history.
Your working copy. Where you write R and Quarto.


Your website
Shows what is in its docs/ folder
Changes here are invisible until you push


Direction
pull brings GitHub’s changes down to Posit Cloud
push sends your commits up to GitHub



The routine is always the same: edit → render → commit → push → check your site.










Word
Meaning




Git
The program that records versions of your files. It runs inside Posit Cloud; you click its buttons in the Git tab.


Commit
A saved snapshot of the files you chose, with a short message saying what changed. It stays in Posit Cloud until you push.


Stage
Tick a file’s box to include it in the next commit.


Push
Send your commits from Posit Cloud up to GitHub.


Pull
Bring commits from GitHub down into Posit Cloud (for example, a change you made on github.com).


Personal access token
A long secret code GitHub gives you to use instead of your password when you push. Treat it exactly like a password.


Render
Run Quarto to turn your .qmd files into the web pages in docs/.

title: Setup, Part 2: Connect Posit Cloud to GitHub
text:
Task
Open your cis-3901-projects project in Posit Cloud (space CIS-3901-Fall2026) and keep this page open in another browser tab, next to a tab on GitHub. Do the steps in order; each takes 5 to 10 minutes.

Step 0. Check the packages (2 to 5 minutes)
Rendering the site needs the tidyverse and rmarkdown. In the Console, run:
needed <- c("tidyverse", "rmarkdown")
needed[!needed %in% rownames(installed.packages())]

If it prints character(0), everything is installed: go to Step A.
If it prints a package name, install what’s missing. This takes a few minutes; wait for the > prompt to come back.

install.packages(c("tidyverse", "rmarkdown"))


Step A. Tell Git who you are (5 minutes)
Every commit is signed with a name and an email. Your repository is public, so use GitHub’s private noreply email instead of your real one.

On GitHub: click your profile picture (top right) › Settings › Emails.
Tick Keep my email addresses private. GitHub then shows your noreply address, which looks like 12345678+your-username@users.noreply.github.com. Copy it.
In Posit Cloud, click the Terminal tab (next to Console). Type these two lines, one at a time, pressing Enter after each. Use your own name (a first name and last initial is fine) and the address you copied, both inside the quotes:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "12345678+your-username@users.noreply.github.com"

Check: type git config --global --list and press Enter. You should see your user.name and user.email.







TipGood to know



You do this once per Posit Cloud project. If you make another project from a Git repository later, repeat this step there.




Step B. Create your token (10 minutes)
GitHub doesn’t accept your password from Posit Cloud. It accepts a personal access token limited to one repository.

Open the token form: Create my CIS-3901 token. It opens GitHub’s form with the name, description, a 60-day expiration and the right permission already filled in. (Without the link: profile picture › Settings › Developer settings › Personal access tokens › Fine-grained tokens › Generate new token.)
Check or set these fields:

Token name: CIS-3901 Posit Cloud
Expiration: 60 days (past the Dec 4 presentations).
Repository access: choose Only select repositories, then pick cis-3901-projects. The link can’t fill this one in for you.
Permissions › Repository permissions › Contents: Read and write. (Metadata: Read-only is added automatically.) Leave everything else as it is.

Click Generate token. GitHub shows the token, starting with github_pat_, only once. Click the copy icon.
Keep it somewhere safe for the next 10 minutes: a password manager is best. If you lose it, you can always make a new one (see If something goes wrong).







WarningA token is a password



Never paste it into a file in your project, a commit message, a chat, an email, Blackboard or an AI tool.
Anyone with it can change your repository. If you think it leaked: GitHub › Settings › Developer settings › Fine-grained tokens › Delete, then create a new one.




Step C. Your first commit and push (10 minutes)

In the Files pane, open index.qmd. Near the top, replace Your Name with your name (again, first name and last initial is fine). Save the file (Ctrl+S, or Cmd+S on a Mac).
Click the Git tab (top-right pane). index.qmd appears with a blue M (modified).
Tick the Staged box next to index.qmd. If you also see a file ending in .Rproj with a yellow ?, tick it too: it’s your project’s settings file.
Click Commit. A Review Changes window opens. In Commit message, type Add my name to the home page, then click Commit. Read the small report, then click Close.
Click the green Push arrow (↑). Posit Cloud asks two questions:

Username: your GitHub username.
Password: paste your token (not your GitHub password). Nothing appears while you paste; that’s normal. Press Enter.

When the report ends with a line like main -> main, click Close.
On GitHub, reload your repository. Near the top you see your commit message and “now” or “1 minute ago”. Click index.qmd: your name is there.







NoteWhy your website hasn’t changed yet



Your site shows the docs/ folder, and docs/ still holds the old rendered page. Step D renders the site so docs/ has your name too.


Posit Cloud remembers your token for up to 12 hours, in memory only (never in a file). After that, or after the project restarts, it asks again: paste the token again.


Step D. Render and publish (10 minutes)

In the Terminal tab, type quarto render and press Enter. Quarto renders each page and reports Output created: docs/index.html at the end (about 1 minute). Or use the Build tab › Render Website.
In the Git tab you now see many changed files in docs/. Click Commit.
In the Review Changes window, click once in the file list, press Ctrl+A (Cmd+A on a Mac), then click Stage. Every box is ticked.
Message: Render site with my name. Click Commit, then Close, then Push (↑), then Close.
Wait 1 to 2 minutes, then open your site: https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/cis-3901-projects/. Reload (Ctrl+Shift+R, or Cmd+Shift+R). Your name is on the home page.



Step E. One habit: pull first (2 minutes)
If you ever change a file on github.com (for example, you fix a typo in README.md there), GitHub has a commit that Posit Cloud doesn’t. Bring it down before you start working: in the Git tab, click the blue Pull arrow (↓).






ImportantYour routine for every work session




Pull (↓).
Edit and save.
Render (quarto render).
Stage and Commit with a clear message.
Push (↑).
Check your site.

Commit small and often. Every commit is a point you can go back to.

git config --global --list shows your name and your noreply email.
Your token is limited to cis-3901-projects, has Contents: Read and write, and expires in about 60 days.
GitHub shows your two commits: Add my name to the home page and Render site with my name.

title: Setup, Part 2: Connect Posit Cloud to GitHub
section: Using GitHub Copilot as a helper (optional)
text:
Using GitHub Copilot as a helper (optional)
GitHub Copilot is GitHub’s AI assistant. Used well, it explains instead of doing: what an error message means, what a Git word means, what a line in a file does. You still click the buttons and make the decisions.
How to get it

Copilot Free comes with every GitHub account, with a monthly limit. Open https://github.com/copilot and start a chat.
Copilot Student (more use, free) requires GitHub Education verification: https://github.com/settings/education/benefits. Approval can take several days, and GitHub has paused new student sign-ups at times in 2026; Copilot Free is enough for this tutorial.
In Posit Cloud (code suggestions as you type): Tools › Global Options › Copilot, tick Enable GitHub Copilot, then sign in with the code it shows. You do this once per project.

Prompts that help

“I’m new to Git. Explain the difference between commit and push in two sentences.”
“I pushed from RStudio and got this message: [paste the message]. What does it mean, and what should I check?”
Open a file on GitHub and ask Copilot: “Explain what _quarto.yml controls in this repository.”







WarningRules




Never share your token with Copilot or any AI tool. Before you paste an error message, check it doesn’t contain a token or your email.
Check what Copilot says against this tutorial. If they disagree, follow the tutorial and ask in office hours.
In graded work, AI use follows that assignment’s AI level (see the AI Use Levels document) and must be logged as it says.

title: Setup, Part 2: Connect Posit Cloud to GitHub
text:
If something goes wrong








What you see
Why
What to do




Authentication failed or Invalid username or token
You typed your GitHub password, or the token was cut off when you copied it.
Push again and paste the whole token (it starts with github_pat_). Still failing: make a new token (Regenerate).


403, Permission denied, or Write access to repository not granted
The token can’t write to this repository.
GitHub › Settings › Developer settings › Fine-grained tokens › your token › Edit: Repository access must include cis-3901-projects; Contents: Read and write. Save, then push again.


Please tell me who you are when you commit
Step A not done in this project.
Do Step A, then commit again.


GH007: Your push would publish a private email address
The commit used your real email while GitHub keeps it private.
Do Step A with the noreply address, then in the Terminal run git commit --amend --reset-author --no-edit and push again.


Push rejected: fetch first or Updates were rejected
GitHub has a commit you don’t have (you edited on github.com).
Click Pull (↓), then Push (↑).


The token stopped working after weeks
It expired.
Fine-grained tokens › your token › Regenerate token, or create a new one as in Step B.


You lost the token
GitHub shows it only once.
Regenerate it, or delete it and create a new one.


Asked for username and token again
Normal: Posit Cloud forgets it after 12 hours or a restart.
Paste the token again.


Commit button does nothing, or nothing to commit
The file isn’t saved, or no box is ticked.
Save (the file name turns black), tick Staged, then Commit.


quarto render says there is no package called ...
A package is missing.
Do Step 0, then render again.


Site still shows Your Name
docs/ wasn’t rendered, staged or pushed; or the browser shows an old copy.
Repeat Step D; reload with Ctrl+Shift+R. On GitHub, the Actions tab shows pages build and deployment finishing.


Site shows 404
Pages is off or set to the wrong folder.
Settings › Pages: Deploy from a branch, main, /docs, Save. Check the address: your username and cis-3901-projects.



Still stuck? Copy the exact message (without any token), take a screenshot, and bring it to office hours or send it through Blackboard. Nothing you do here can break the course template, and GitHub keeps every commit, so mistakes can be undone.

title: Setup, Part 2: Connect Posit Cloud to GitHub
text:
Check yourself (not graded)

You edited index.qmd and pushed, but your site didn’t change. What step was missing?
Why do you use a token instead of your GitHub password when you push from Posit Cloud?
You fixed a typo in README.md on github.com. What do you click in Posit Cloud before you start working?
Does a commit change anything on GitHub by itself?
Where is it safe to keep your token: a text file in your project, a password manager, or a Blackboard post?
Why use your noreply email for commits?



Show the answers


Render (quarto render), then commit and push the changed docs/ files.
GitHub doesn’t accept passwords from Git. A token can be limited to one repository and one permission, and it expires.
Pull (↓).
No: a commit stays in Posit Cloud until you push.
A password manager only.
Your repository is public, and every commit shows its email; noreply keeps your real address private.
